main.title: Super Monaco GP
main.summary: Super Monaco GP is a Formula One racing simulation video game released by Sega, originally as a Sega X Board arcade game in 1989, followed by ports for multiple video game consoles and home computers in the early 1990s.

cards.text: Super Monaco GP is a Formula One racing simulation video game released by Sega, originally as a Sega X Board arcade game in 1989, followed by ports for multiple video game consoles and home computers in the early 1990s. It is the sequel to the 1979 arcade game Monaco GP. The arcade game consists of one race, the Monaco Grand Prix, but later ports added more courses and game modes based on the 1989 Formula One World Championship.

The original concept for Super Monaco GP came from Hisao Oguchi, who was at the time a game planner with Sega. The arcade game contained parodies of actual brands that were sponsors in Formula One, which led to a lawsuit from Philip Morris over advertising of tobacco products. Shortly after the arcade game launch, Super Monaco GP was ported to Sega's video game consoles, the Genesis, Master System, and Game Gear. British developer U.S. Gold published ports for home computers.

The arcade game was a major worldwide hit; in Japan, it was the third highest-grossing arcade game of 1989 and then the highest-grossing dedicated arcade game of 1990. The arcade and Genesis versions received positive reviews from critics, focused on the game's graphics and playability. Ports for 8-bit systems ranged from mixed to generally favorable depending on the platforms, with the conversions less well received for their difficulty and differences in gameplay.

main.title: Big Run
main.summary: Big Run is a rally racing arcade video game released by Jaleco in 1989.

cards.text: Big Run is Jaleco's 1989 arcade rally-racing game. Its pseudo-3D route follows the Paris-Dakar rally, with the player driving a Porsche 959 resembling the 1986 winner. Rival vehicles resemble the Peugeot 205 T16, which won in 1987, and occasionally Mitsubishi Pajeros.
Big Run was also converted to the Amiga and Atari ST by The Sales Curve.

The race proceeds in a straight line without any 360° effects to simulate about turns in the road. Most of the turns are at a 30° angle, forcing the player to turn sharply to the left or right. At the end of the game, a message reads: "Those who have tasted the waters of Africa will always long to be here", accompanied by synthesized beats. This message plays after the "game over" screen in the event of either winning or losing the game.

The object of the game is to travel from Tripoli, Libya, through the swamp regions of West Africa to Dakar in a rally race. Players must finish each leg of the rally before time runs out; failing to achieve this goal will result in disqualification and an immediate game over, as in the real life rally circuit. Hitting various environmental obstacles or other vehicles damages the player's vehicle. Receiving too much damage results in problems with the vehicle's components. Other challenges include difficult terrain, deserts, jungles, and darkness.

Players can choose their own navigators, corporate sponsors, auto mechanics, and automobile parts during the race of over 4,000 kilometres or 2,500 miles. Navigators help by directing players safely past areas of darkness in the race. Engine parts must be replaced by mechanics approximately every 2,500 kilometres or 1,600 miles. Racing equipment (tires, engine, brakes) must be packed up in the vehicle, creating extra weight that reduces the vehicle's top speed. The goal is to have as many replacement parts as possible while keeping the vehicle as light as possible. Emergencies do not cost money but cause the player to lose time while waiting for the repair truck. Having no parts eventually causes the vehicle to stall on the rally, also wasting the player's time.

In Japan, Game Machine listed Big Run on their November 15, 1989, issue as being the second most-successful upright arcade game of the month. It went on to become Japan's fourth highest-grossing dedicated arcade game of 1990, below Super Monaco GP, Winning Run Suzuka GP and Special Criminal Investigation. In North America, it was the top-grossing new video game on the RePlay arcade charts in January 1990.

main.title: Populous
main.summary: Populous is a video game developed by Bullfrog Productions and published by Electronic Arts for the Amiga in March 1989, then quickly the Atari ST and MS-DOS.

cards.heading: A god game reaches home computers
cards.text: Populous is a video game developed by Bullfrog Productions and published by Electronic Arts for the Amiga in March 1989, then quickly the Atari ST and MS-DOS. Many conversions followed, including for the Genesis, Super NES, and PC Engine consoles. Populous is considered the first god game. With over four million copies sold, Populous is one of the best-selling PC games of all time.

cards.heading: Shaping the land to guide its people
cards.text: The player assumes the role of a deity, who must lead followers through direction, manipulation, and divine intervention, with the goal of eliminating the followers led by the opposite deity. Played from an isometric perspective, the game consists of more than 500 levels, with each level being a piece of land which contains the player's followers and the enemy's followers. The player is tasked with defeating the enemy followers and increasing their own followers' population using a series of divine powers before moving on to the next level. The game was designed by Peter Molyneux, and Bullfrog developed a gameplay prototype via a board game they invented using Lego.

cards.heading: An idea that becomes a series
cards.text: The game received critical acclaim upon release, with critics praising the game's graphics, design, sounds and replay value. It was nominated for multiple year-end accolades, including Game of the Year from several gaming publications. Retrospectively, it has been considered one of the greatest video games of all time. The game was ported to many other computer systems and was later supported with multiple expansion packs. It is the first game in the Populous series, preceding Populous II: Trials of the Olympian Gods and Populous: The Beginning.

main.title: Clash at Demonhead
main.subtitle: Vic Tokai · Nintendo Entertainment System
main.summary: Clash at Demonhead is Vic Tokai's NES action adventure, starring special agent Billy 'Big Bang' Blitz. A kidnapped scientist and a doomsday weapon send him through a network of routes containing enemies, allies and unexpected diversions. Bang runs, jumps and fires a gun, but the map gives those familiar actions a more open structure. Junctions offer different destinations, and earlier areas can be revisited. The mission develops through encounters spread across that network, gradually explaining which person or object should be found next.

cards.heading: A rescue with a map of its own
cards.text: Clash at Demonhead is Vic Tokai's NES action adventure, starring special agent Billy 'Big Bang' Blitz. A kidnapped scientist and a doomsday weapon send him through a network of routes containing enemies, allies and unexpected diversions. Bang runs, jumps and fires a gun, but the map gives those familiar actions a more open structure. Junctions offer different destinations, and earlier areas can be revisited. The mission develops through encounters spread across that network, gradually explaining which person or object should be found next.

cards.heading: Buy equipment for the route ahead
cards.text: Shops offer weapons and equipment that help Bang manage the changing terrain. Later powers include flight, healing, shrinking and travel back to previously visited locations. These abilities give a practical reason to remember a difficult stretch rather than treat it as finished once passed. The world contains more than forty routes, making the choice of direction part of play. Some journeys advance the main mission; others provide the resources or information that make the next attempt more promising.

cards.heading: The strange company along the way
cards.text: The story introduces a skeletal mastermind, a captured hermit and several unreliable acquaintances as Bang pursues the medallions associated with the bomb. Conversations change the meaning of places already visited and send the player toward another part of the map. Its humour comes partly from putting a confident action hero in situations he cannot solve merely by shooting. Released in Japan as Dengeki Big Bang!, the game uses a succession of eccentric meetings to give its open routes a reason to be followed.

main.title: Military Madness
main.subtitle: A lunar war measured in turns
main.summary: Military Madness is Hudson's turn-based strategy game, first released in Japan as Nectaris on 9 February 1989.

cards.heading: A lunar war measured in turns
cards.text: Military Madness is Hudson's turn-based strategy game, first released in Japan as Nectaris on 9 February 1989. A war on the Moon in 2089 places the Allied-Union against the Axis-Xenon Empire, whose missile threatens Earth. The player commands a fixed force across hexagonal maps, aiming to occupy an enemy prison camp or eliminate opposing units. Each battlefield is a compact military problem: where to move, which enemy to engage and how to protect the units needed for the next stage of the advance.

cards.heading: The strength of a formation
cards.text: Terrain affects ground movement and the outcome of combat, while nearby friendly units strengthen one another. A strong position therefore depends on the shape of the formation as well as the type of vehicle involved. Units gain experience through fighting, giving survival value beyond the immediate encounter. Capturing factories brings access to stored equipment and repairs, so controlling a useful site can change the balance of the map. The player has to coordinate these advantages before an exposed vehicle becomes the opponent's easiest target.

cards.heading: A small battlefield with lasting influence
cards.text: Sixteen basic maps lead to a harder set, with passwords allowing the campaign to continue between sessions. A tutorial explains the rules, and a two-player mode lets another person command the opposition. Jun Chikuma composed the music. The game later reached numerous platforms and was cited as an influence on Dune II. Its original PC Engine release demonstrates how a clear map, a limited set of units and carefully connected combat bonuses can produce a substantial strategy game within a compact console presentation.

main.title: Famicom Jump: Hero Retsuden
main.summary: Famicom Jump: Hero Retsuden (the subtitle translates to "Heroes History") is a 1989 role-playing video game for the Family Computer published by Bandai.

cards.text: Famicom Jump: Hero Retsuden (the subtitle translates to "Heroes History") is a 1989 role-playing video game for the Family Computer published by Bandai. The game commemorates the 20th anniversary of Shueisha's manga anthology Weekly Shōnen Jump.

The game is set in a world that brings together many of the long-running titles, which include stories of the past and present at the time of their release, that had appeared in the magazine.  The game consists of a main character wandering and encountering the many Jump heroes as they try to save the world from an alliance of many of the most powerful and evil of the Jump villains.
The game sold 1.1 million cartridges for the Famicom in Japan. It was the first title in the Jump video game series. It had a sequel, Famicom Jump II: Saikyō no Shichinin.

main.title: Dungeon Explorer
main.summary: Dungeon Explorer is an action role-playing video game developed by Atlus for the TurboGrafx-16 and originally published by Hudson Soft in Japan on March 4, 1989, and later in North America by NEC on November 15 of the same year.

cards.text: Dungeon Explorer is an action role-playing video game developed by Atlus for the TurboGrafx-16 and originally published by Hudson Soft in Japan on March 4, 1989, and later in North America by NEC on November 15 of the same year. The first installment in the eponymous franchise, the game is set in the land of Oddesia, which has been overrun by an alien race and where players assume the role of one of eight main characters tasked with recovering the Ora stone to kill the alien king Natas. Co-directed by Kazutoshi Ueda and Yōsuke Niino, the title was created by most of the same team that would work on later several projects such as entries in the Megami Tensei series. Though it was initially launched for the TurboGrafx-16, it was later re-released through download services for various consoles.

Dungeon Explorer garnered positive reception from critics during its initial release and is considered a pioneer title in the action role-playing game genre due to its co-operative multiplayer gameplay for up to five players, but has been met with a more mixed response from reviewers in recent years. It was followed by four sequels: Dungeon Explorer II (1993), Dungeon Explorer for Sega CD and Crystal Beans from Dungeon Explorer (1995), as well as Dungeon Explorer: Warriors of Ancient Arts (2007).

main.title: Strider
main.summary: Strider, released in Japan as Strider Hiryū, is a 1989 hack and slash platform game developed and published by Capcom for arcades.

cards.text: Strider, released in Japan as Strider Hiryū, is a 1989 hack and slash platform game developed and published by Capcom for arcades. Set in a dystopian future in which Earth is ruled by the tyrannical Grandmaster Meio, it follows the titular Strider named Hiryu as he attempts to end Meio's tyrannical reign for good. The game resulted from cooperation between Capcom and manga publisher Moto Kikaku. It marked the video game debut of Strider Hiryu, after the character was introduced in the 1988 manga Strider Hiryū.

The game debuted on Capcom's CP System arcade board. Various home computer ports were developed by Tiertex and published by U.S. Gold in 1989. The NES version has a different plot than the original. Sega released Strider for its own Genesis console in 1990. Of all home versions, the Genesis adaptation is considered the most successful, winning the Game of the Year and Best Graphics in a Video Game awards from Electronic Gaming Monthly in 1990.

Strider's gameplay is cited as a major influence on the video game franchises Ninja Gaiden, Devil May Cry, and God of War. It became one of Capcom's early hits, praised for its innovative gameplay, diverse and unique music, and multilingual voice samples.

main.title: Phantasy Star II
main.summary: Phantasy Star II is a science fantasy  role-playing video game developed and published by Sega for the Sega Genesis.

cards.text: Phantasy Star II is a science fantasy  role-playing video game developed and published by Sega for the Sega Genesis. It was released in Japan in 1989 and North America and Europe in 1990. It was later ported to a variety of different platforms. An updated remake, Phantasy Star Generation 2, was released for the PlayStation 2 in 2005 in Japan.

Phantasy Star II is the second installment in Sega's acclaimed Phantasy Star series and serves as a sequel to the original Phantasy Star for the Master System. Phantasy Star II takes place 1,000 years after the events of its predecessor and follows the journey of a government agent named Rolf and his friends, who are on a mission to discover why the protector of the planet Mota, Mother Brain, has started malfunctioning.

Phantasy Star II was the first video game to use a 6 mega-bit cartridge, making it the biggest video game on a console at the time. Since its release Phantasy Star II has been the subject of critical acclaim.

main.title: Game Boy
main.subtitle: The Console That Turned Dead Time into Play Time
main.summary: Nintendo made portable play a balance of battery life, size, controls and games. Game Boy's modest display was one part of that choice.

cards.heading: The Console That Turned Dead Time into Play Time
cards.text: Nintendo launched Game Boy in Japan on April 21, 1989. Gunpei Yokoi's pragmatic approach combined mature technology, interchangeable cartridges and portable controls with battery life, durability and price. Tetris became a close companion to the machine, while Pokémon later made trading through the Link Cable part of its appeal. Games could travel with the player instead of remaining at the television.

cards.heading: Choosing Mature Technology Over Spectacle
cards.text: Game Boy's monochrome display reduced demands on power, cost and size. Weight, battery life and durability mattered when the console was carried through an ordinary day. Nintendo chose familiar components that could work together in a reliable portable object. The resulting balance helped determine how often owners could use it away from home.

cards.heading: Tetris Shows Why a Match Belongs in a Pocket
cards.text: Tetris fits sessions that may last a few minutes or a whole journey. Its visible puzzle is easy to recognise when play resumes, making it suited to the interruptions of portable use. The pairing gave Game Boy an immediately understandable activity beyond demonstrating the machine's hardware.

cards.heading: The Link Cable Builds a Network Before the Internet
cards.text: The Game Link Cable physically connects two nearby Game Boys for compatible games. Pokémon later gave the connection a central role through creature trading, with a complete collection depending on exchange. Players needed two machines, a cable and time together. A feature built into portable hardware became a reason to arrange a shared meeting.

features.title: Finding the game inside a limit

cards.heading: Seventy-two parts of a screen
cards.text: The Game & Watch developers' Nintendo interview makes a hardware limit countable. Ball used a chip able to control seventy-two display segments. Twenty-eight served the four-digit counter, leaving forty-four for the character and balls. These were shaped elements that could be switched on or off, rather than a freely drawn pixel image. Gunpei Yokoi and Satoru Okada were already making the prototype when Makoto Kano joined. The product's clarity emerged from choosing what those limited shapes should show, not from promising that the screen could depict anything.

cards.heading: A notebook instead of a legend
cards.text: Notes from an ideas meeting preserve suggestions for Game & Watch, including Chef. In Nintendo's interview, colleagues described many people contributing proposals before Yokoi simplified them and concentrated the activity. Makoto Kano had joined after development began, so the working documents and team recollections describe the process more directly than the familiar calculator-on-a-train origin story.

cards.heading: Start with a feeling
cards.text: Yoshio Sakamoto recalled Yokoi proposing a floating sensation combined with fighting for Balloon Fight. Sakamoto drew and designed the game; SRD programmed the arcade version, and Satoru Iwata worked on the home version. The proposed feeling guided several people as they translated it into images, movement and code.

cards.heading: Try drawing the bubble
cards.text: Sakamoto initially thought a transparent-looking bubble would be impossible with the available graphics. Yokoi asked him to try drawing it before abandoning the idea. Experiments with the development tool produced a workable image. The recollection captures a specific decision reached through testing what the hardware could communicate.

features.title: Hirokazu Tanaka works between music and hardware
features.summary: Engineering and composition meet in the same hands.

cards.heading: A composer works inside the machine
cards.text: Listening to Super Mario Land at a 2014 talk, Hirokazu Tanaka remembered how many jobs overlapped. He had been composing and programming while also working on Game Boy sound hardware and several games. The music did not simply arrive after someone else had finished the machine. The person writing a melody also knew the system producing it. His recollection puts the familiar idea of a soundtrack beside another kind of creative work: deciding what sounds a small device could make.

cards.heading: Small changes open different sounds
cards.text: Tanaka recalled seeking more expression from a sound system constrained by portable size and cost. Left and right output, short sounds and different kinds of noise offered useful choices. Placement and timing could change an effect even with a restricted set of available tones. His hardware knowledge fed directly into composition and sound programming.

cards.heading: The entrance needs another mood
cards.text: Asked later about Metroid, Tanaka described wanting music and effects appropriate to its setting. He also explained why Brinstar began with a lighter mood: the opening needed to help someone enter the game. That makes contrast important within an otherwise unsettling world. An area can welcome a player before another makes them uneasy. When asked how particular effects were made, he gave a practical answer about continuing to program until satisfied, rather than offering a hidden formula for every sound.

cards.heading: An interview corrects a familiar story
cards.text: Tanaka also corrected a story that Nintendo had disliked Metroid's dark sound. He explained that this came from a mistranslation: he had imagined the response sales staff might have, rather than received that feedback. His account separates an anticipated objection during composition from an actual instruction given to the team.

cards.heading: The light around the screen
cards.text: The original Game Boy manual recommends good light and a direct view of the screen. The contrast dial adjusts the darkness of the picture, and a blank-looking display may simply need that setting changed. Portable play depends partly on where the owner holds the machine and the light falling on its reflective screen.

cards.heading: Watching the power fade
cards.text: A dimming indicator and weakening sound warn that Game Boy's four AA batteries need replacement. The manual notes that playing time varies with the game and temperature. Owners must watch the device as well as the game, adjusting contrast or volume and keeping replacement cells available for the next session.

cards.heading: Six cells in the case
cards.text: The original Lynx uses six AA batteries, with its manual estimating about four hours from alkaline cells. It also offers mains power and a car adaptor. Taking the handheld on a journey can therefore involve choosing a power source alongside the game cards to carry.

cards.heading: A pause has a cost
cards.text: On batteries, the original Lynx automatically shuts down after four minutes without use. With an AC adaptor, the manual allows approximately an hour. The different intervals conserve portable power while giving a connected machine longer to remain idle. Even the length of a pause depends on how the console is supplied.
